title: SQL: indexes and reading EXPLAIN
seriesDescription: Joins, aggregates, window functions and CTEs, indexes and EXPLAIN, ACID and isolation, locking. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: B-tree, composite (leftmost prefix), covering, partial and GIN/JSONB indexes, expression indexes, selectivity, and how to read EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE: seq vs index scan, costs, estimates vs actuals. Plans checked on PostgreSQL 16.
source: PostgreSQL 16 documentation (indexes, operator classes, pg_trgm, EXPLAIN, planner cost constants); Use The Index, Luke; Citus and Crunchy Data blogs on EXPLAIN

questions.prompt: Match each PostgreSQL index type to the workload it suits best.

right.text: Equality, range and `ORDER BY` on one or more columns
Containment and search on jsonb, arrays and full-text (`@>`, `@@`)
Very large, naturally ordered tables such as append-only timestamps, with a tiny index
Substring search with `LIKE '%abc%'` with no extension

questions.explanation: B-tree is the default and covers most OLTP needs. GIN is an inverted index (value -> rows). BRIN stores min/max per block range, so it only helps when physical order correlates with the column. A trigram GIN (`pg_trgm`) is needed for `%abc%` searches.

Clauses 1, 3, 4 and 6 constrain a, so the tree can be descended directly (in 4 only a narrows the range; c is just a filter inside it). Clauses 2 and 5 lack the leading column and, at best, scan the whole index.

questions.prompt:
Table `orders` has 1,000,000 rows and 2% of them have `status = 'pending'`. How many entries does

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'
```

contain?
questions.explanation: A partial index stores entries only for rows that satisfy its predicate: 2% of 1,000,000 = 20,000. It is smaller, cheaper to maintain and cacheable, but the query must repeat (or imply) the predicate to use it.

questions.prompt: A table occupies 1,000 pages and holds 100,000 rows. With the default planner constants (`seq_page_cost = 1.0`, `cpu_tuple_cost = 0.01`, `cpu_operator_cost = 0.0025`), what total cost does `EXPLAIN` show for a `Seq Scan` with a `WHERE` filter that applies one comparison operator to every row?
questions.explanation: Cost = pages * 1.0 + rows * 0.01 + rows * 0.0025 = 1000 + 1000 + 250 = 2250. Checked on PostgreSQL: a 1,137-page, 100,000-row table shows cost 2137.00 unfiltered and 2387.00 with one filter operator. Costs are unitless planner estimates, not milliseconds.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: An index on `(customer_id, created_at)` serves `WHERE customer_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10` without a separate sort step.
questions.reason: Entries with the same customer_id are stored in created_at order, and a B-tree can be scanned backwards.

whys.a: Correct: R describes why the index delivers rows already in the requested order.
whys.b: R is the mechanism behind A, so it does explain it.
whys.c: R is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.
whys.d: A is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.

questions.explanation: `EXPLAIN` shows "`Index Scan Backward using ... Index Cond: (customer_id = 5)`" under a Limit node. Put equality columns first, then the sort column.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A B-tree index on `status` always speeds up `WHERE status = 'done'` when 98% of the rows have that value.
questions.reason: The planner compares estimated costs and chooses a sequential scan when a query reads a large fraction of the table.

whys.a: A is false, so both-true options are wrong.
whys.b: A is false, so both-true options are wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.
whys.d: Correct: A is false because reading 98% of the rows through an index (random page access) is slower than a sequential scan; R is true.

questions.explanation: On a 100,000-row test table the planner chose `Seq Scan` for `status = 'done'` (98% of rows) but an index scan for the rare `status = 'pending'`. Low-cardinality columns are poor stand-alone B-tree keys; consider a partial index on the rare value.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: `WHERE lower(email) = 'ana@example.com'` cannot use a plain B-tree index on the column `email`.
questions.reason: An expression index on `lower(email)` can serve that predicate.

whys.a: R is a fix for the problem, not the cause of the limitation in A.
whys.b: Correct: both are true; A holds because the index stores email, not `lower(email)`, and R is the remedy.
whys.c: R is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.
whys.d: A is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.

questions.explanation: Checked on PostgreSQL: `Seq Scan` before `CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email))`, `Index Scan` after. Alternatives: `citext`, or normalise the value when storing it.

questions.text: CREATE INDEX ON t (a) {1} (b) stores column b in the index leaf entries, so an {2} Scan can answer the query without visiting the heap. That only works for pages marked all-visible in the {3} map, which VACUUM maintains.
questions.explanation: Included columns are not part of the search key, so they cannot be used for seeking or ordering, but they avoid heap fetches. "`Heap Fetches: N`" in `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows how often the visibility map did not help.

questions.prompt: Table `orders(id, tenant_id, status, created_at, total)`. The hot query is `WHERE tenant_id = ? AND status = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`. Write the `CREATE INDEX` statement that serves it with no extra sort.

checks.label: puts the two equality columns first, then created_at

questions.model:
CREATE INDEX orders_tenant_status_created
  ON orders (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC);
questions.explanation: Equality columns first (in either order), range/sort column last. `created_at DESC` is optional because a B-tree can be scanned backwards.

questions.prompt: Table `orders(id, status, created_at)`. Only about 2% of the rows are `'pending'` and a job polls them ordered by creation time. Write the statement that creates a partial index on `created_at` covering only pending rows.
questions.explanation: The polling query must contain `status = 'pending'` for the planner to prove the partial index applies. Same trick: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` for soft deletes.

questions.prompt: Table `orders` has a `jsonb` column `attrs`. Write the statement that creates a GIN index on it, then a query selecting the orders whose `attrs` contain `{"tag": "vip"}` in a way that index can serve.

checks.label: creates a GIN index on attrs

questions.model:
CREATE INDEX orders_attrs_gin ON orders USING gin (attrs);
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE attrs @> '{"tag": "vip"}';
questions.explanation: The default `jsonb_ops` class supports `@>, ?, ?| and ?&`. `jsonb_path_ops` is smaller and faster for `@>` only. `->>` equality (`attrs->>'tag' = 'vip'`) needs an expression B-tree index instead. Checked on PostgreSQL: `Bitmap Index Scan` on the GIN index.

questions.prompt:
An index on `orders(customer_id, created_at)` exists.

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id::text = '5'
```

shows

```text
"Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..2887.00 rows=500 width=54)
  Filter: ((customer_id)::text = '5'::text)".
```

Why was the index not used?

options.text: The cast on customer_id blocks index use; compare customer_id = 5 instead.
options.why: Right: wrapping an indexed column in a function or cast prevents index use unless an expression index exists.

options.text: The table is too small, because PostgreSQL never uses an index below one million rows.
options.why: There is no such threshold; the planner is purely cost based.

options.text: A composite index is only usable when every one of its columns appears in the `WHERE` clause of the query.
options.why: A leading-column condition is enough; the other columns can be omitted.

options.text: Casts to text need `enable_indexscan` to be switched on for that session.
options.why: `enable_indexscan` is on by default and unrelated to the cast.

questions.explanation: Same family of traps: `WHERE` date(created_at) = ..., `WHERE` col + 1 = ..., implicit casts caused by mismatched parameter types, and `LIKE` with a leading wildcard.

questions.prompt:
`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows

```text
"Seq Scan on orders (cost=0.00..2387.00 rows=10 width=54) (actual time=0.02..18.4 rows=48210 loops=1)
  Filter: (status = 'done'::text)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 51790".
```

What does the gap between `rows=10` and `rows=48210` most likely mean, and what do you try first?

options.text: Statistics are stale or missing; run `ANALYZE` and check autovacuum.
options.why: Right: a 4,800x misestimate leads to bad join orders and scan choices.

options.text: The index on status is corrupt, so run `REINDEX` immediately to repair it and force its use.
options.why: The plan does not use an index, and nothing in it hints at corruption.

options.text: `work_mem` is too low; raise it so the scan returns more rows.
options.why: `work_mem` affects sorts and hashes, not row estimates.

options.text: The table is bloated; `VACUUM FULL` will fix the estimate.
options.why: Bloat changes page counts, not the selectivity estimate for a column.

questions.explanation: Always compare estimated and actual rows per node. If `ANALYZE` does not help, look at correlated columns (`CREATE STATISTICS`) or a higher statistics target for skewed columns.

questions.prompt: Select all true statements about `EXPLAIN` and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` in PostgreSQL.

options.text: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually executes the statement, so wrap `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE` in `BEGIN ... ROLLBACK`.
options.why: Right: otherwise the data change really happens.

options.text: Cost numbers are unitless planner estimates, not milliseconds.
options.why: Right: use actual time from `ANALYZE` for real durations.

options.text: Comparing estimated rows with actual rows per node reveals bad statistics.
options.why: Right: large gaps explain wrong plan choices.

options.text: Plain `EXPLAIN` runs the query and reports real timings.
options.why: Plain `EXPLAIN` only plans; it needs `ANALYZE` to execute.

options.text: A lower total cost always means the query will run faster.
options.why: Costs are estimates; wrong statistics or caching can invert the ordering.

questions.explanation: Add `BUFFERS` to see shared hit/read counts: it shows whether a query is CPU-bound or I/O-bound.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL a B-tree index stores entries for `NULL` values, so `WHERE col IS NULL` can use the index.

options.why: Right: PostgreSQL B-trees index NULLs (sorted last by default).
It can: NULLs are indexed in PostgreSQL, so `IS NULL` can use a B-tree index.

questions.explanation: Oracle differs: a single-column B-tree does not index rows whose key is entirely `NULL`, so `IS NULL` cannot use it there (a composite index with a non-null column, or a function-based index, works around it). Checked on PostgreSQL: a `Bitmap Index Scan` was used for `IS NULL`.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: In a database whose default collation is not C, a plain B-tree index on a text column cannot serve `WHERE col LIKE 'abc%'`.
questions.reason: An index created with the `text_pattern_ops` operator class compares strings character by character and can serve left-anchored `LIKE` patterns.

whys.a: R does not explain A: A is about the default operator class following locale sort rules, while R merely names the fix.
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but R is the remedy, not the reason. Locale-aware ordering is why the default index cannot turn a prefix match into a range.
whys.c: R is true (`text_pattern_ops` exists for exactly this), so calling it false is wrong.
whys.d: A is true on locale collations (verified: `Seq Scan` on 100,000 rows, `Index Only Scan` after `text_pattern_ops`), so calling it false is wrong.

questions.explanation: Checked on PostgreSQL 16: with an en_US-style collation, `LIKE 'abc%'` did a `Seq Scan` on a plain index; after `CREATE INDEX ... (x text_pattern_ops)` the planner used `Index Cond x ~>=~ 'abc' AND x ~<~ 'abd'`. A database created with the C collation, or a trigram GIN index (`pg_trgm`), are alternatives; `%abc%` still needs trigrams.

questions.prompt: Table `products(id, name text)`. Write the statements that let `WHERE name ILIKE '%shoe%'` use an index in PostgreSQL (assume you may install extensions).

checks.label: creates a GIN (or GiST) index on name

questions.model:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
CREATE INDEX products_name_trgm ON products USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops);
questions.explanation: A B-tree cannot help with a leading wildcard because the match is not a prefix. `pg_trgm` splits strings into three-character grams; the GIN index supports `LIKE`, `ILIKE` and regex searches. GiST with `gist_trgm_ops` also works and additionally supports nearest-neighbour similarity ordering.
